Suspension should be set up for the following: small bump compliance, mid stroke support, and bottom out resistance. Sag is kinda irrelevant, and is mostly just a guideline for your initial pre-tweaked suspension setup. It's always going to be a compromise depending on which of those 3 factors you need the most. 

You don't have to change it for every trail, but it does sound like you're running your suspension pretty hard right now. I'd take out some pressure, and add some token if you're worried about bottom-outs.

I was actually thinking about this question/answer before you even asked! I was considering adding "bump absorption" to the things you want in suspension, but it's so obvious it's kind of a given. The reason you run 170mm over 100mm is because you want it to absorb bigger bumps, or more bumps at a higher speed. If you're not regularly using the majority of your travel it points to two things: your suspension isn't properly set up (which I'm about to get to), or you're just plain overgunned (like a freeride bike on a flat trail).

If you're only using 75% (not on a paved road, but a regular MTB ride), that will usually mean you have great midstroke support, an excess of bottom out resistance (you're not coming close to a bottom out), and a definite lack of small bump sensitivity, which is needed for comfort, braking, and grip. To a dirt jumper who doesn't need much grip but needs a ton of support and doesn't want to bottom out this isn't a problem. For a regular rider it's not ideal.

Suspension is designed around the idea that you'll use almost all of the travel. A rule of thumb is you want the gnarliest feature on your regular trails to use 90%+ of your travel, while avoiding a harsh bottom out. Regular stuff will be going to around 80% travel, and really tame stuff will probably stay under 50%. And bear in mind 20-30% is already used from passive, loaded sag.

> Basically I'm looking for more small bump compliance. 

Small bump compliance = less air pressure, and less compression damping. If you're only using 80% of travel with only 1 token, I'd say it's your air pressure that's too high.

> Past that I'm looking for the bike to stay firm in the corners,

The exact opposite :/. For support in corners you need low speed compression damping, and adequate air pressure.

> I like my bike to soak the terrain up.

Again, that means you want small bump compliance as well as fully used travel = less air pressure.

The last part is a bit iffy. Yes I would take out the token, but I wouldn't *increase* LSC after that. LSC isn't going to have much bearing on your final 20% of travel. I'd try running compression damping completely open and checking if you have enough support in corners. If you do you can probably lower air pressure a bit.

NOTE: The RS Pike has had issues with small bump compliance for lighter riders (say 160 lbs). Apparently the shim stacks is fukt for anyone other than a honkin' 200lb clyde. To change this you need a custom tune, or something like the Vorsprung Luftkappe, or both. My front and rear setups are very different because I found the Pike setup so damn difficult. Rear Deluxe has maxed tokens and 31%-ish sag. Pike has closer to 18% sag, no tokens, and open damping, and I use around 90% of travel on most rides (but I still do bottom out on occasion when I land poorly). With the Pike I had to favour support over small bumps, because if I get it real smooth the fork dives all over the place. 

Also note: tire pressure makes a big difference for grip. 25psi vs. 20psi should be immediately noticeable. On normal tires I would keep PSI as low as possible without getting rim strikes from your tire bottoming out or excessive squirm, and without going under 20psi. The rolling resistance increase from lower PSI is actually pretty minimal above 20psi. A study found a 3.1% reduction in rolling speed going from 40psi to 20psi, which is nothing unless you're XC racing. https://www.singletracks.com/blog/mtb-training/how-does-mtb-tire-pressure-affect-power-and-speed-searching-for-the-perfect-tire-pressure/

A few things:

Rigid bikes aren't really going to improve your riding. If anything it'll be more punishing if you make a mistake, thus making it harder to learn (because you'll be scared of getting hurt). The whole "it teaches you to choose better lines" is a fallacy. Line choice is entirely dependant on the type of bike you're on. Rigid bikes will choose even smoother (and probably slower) lines. Full-suspension bikes are best at finding the very fastest downhill lines.

Full-suspension bikes tend to be better technical climbers too (provided they don't wallow). The suspension helps prevent getting hung up on roots 'n' such.

Full-suspension bikes do have more maintenance, but also ask yourself how often you're servicing pivots and your shock. For me it's not very often. For riders in a specific region it's probably a lot more often.

That's not to say rigid bikes can't be equal amounts of fun. They're better at jumping, pumping, and hopping, and have the most efficient pedalling. They're also cheaper, simpler, usually lighter, and require very little maintenance. However, their grip, braking, comfort, and wheel-sparing abilities are worse.
